title: A Tiny Red Plant With a Death Hug
summary:
Hidden beside sinkhole lakes in Florida's Panhandle lives a small carnivorous plant with dazzling red, thread-like leaves ending in tightly coiled spirals. It is the Florida threadleaf sundew, officially recognized as its own species, Drosera floridana, in August 2026.

Florida botanist Lilly Anderson-Messec first saw the plant in 2014 and thought how different and unique it looked. It was then classified as a variety of the widespread thread-leaved sundew, but she was not convinced, partly because the closest population of that sundew was hundreds of miles away in South Carolina.

Noah Juve, now an undergraduate at the University of Florida, published the description that elevated it to species status. With co-author Andreas Fleischmann of the Munich Herbarium, Juve spent years comparing it with relatives at more than 100 coastal sites. It stood out for its red color, seed shape, flower shape and bloom time.

Its hunting style earned a dramatic nickname: the slow-motion death hug. Sticky droplets work like flypaper, trapping small insects; the plant wraps around them and releases digestive enzymes that slowly break the prey down.

Its home is just as fragile. The sundew grows only on sandy sinkhole-lake margins in a patch about 12 miles by 16 miles, smaller than Chicago, in just two Florida counties, Washington and Bay, making it the most range-restricted sundew in the United States. The lakes formed over thousands to millions of years as acidic rain dissolved limestone, and seeping groundwater creates thin, acidic, nutrient-poor layers along white quartz sand shores.

University of Florida senior Galen Bodner spent months searching and remembers thousands of sundews glowing pink in sunlight. Naming matters for its future: plants ranked only as a subspecies or variety stay hidden from conservation, Fleischmann explained, and as Juve put it, "If something doesn't have a name, how can you conserve it?"
why_it_matters: Naming a rare plant is the first step to protecting it, and this sundew shows how much life can depend on one small, fragile place.
